mcq.prompt: `max(3, 5)` and `max(2.5, 7.1)` are calls to the same function template. What does the compiler produce?
choices: One function that boxes its arguments into a common runtime representation
Two separate instantiations with concrete parameter types, optimised independently
One function plus a runtime type tag that selects the comparison
One function using virtual dispatch on the argument type
mcq.explain: Each distinct set of template arguments generates a separate function at compile time, so `max<int>` and `max<double>` are as concrete as hand-written overloads and can be inlined and optimised separately. The boxing answer describes type erasure — the model behind commonly used Java generics — which is precisely what C++ templates do not do, and why an instantiation costs nothing at runtime.

mcq.prompt: A template body uses `a < b`. The definition compiles cleanly. What does that prove?
choices: Nothing about particular types: operations that depend on `T` are only validated when an instantiation asks for them
That the compiler has already generated code for the common built-in types
That any failure will be reported as a link error rather than a compile error
That every type the template could be called with supports `<`
mcq.explain: The compiler parses the definition when it sees it, but it cannot check `a < b` until it knows what `T` is. That is why an error for a specific type surfaces at the *first use* that instantiates the template, often far from the definition. The name of this hazard is that a template body is not proof that every possible instantiation is valid.

mcq.prompt: Given `template<class T> using Vec = std::vector<T>;`, what is the relationship between `Vec<int>` and `std::vector<int>`?
choices: `Vec<int>` is a derived class of `std::vector<int>`
They are distinct types that convert to each other implicitly
`Vec<int>` is a new, distinct type that wraps `std::vector<int>`
`Vec<int>` is exactly `std::vector<int>` — an alias template creates aliases, not new types
mcq.explain: An alias template names a family of type aliases; the two spellings denote one and the same type, so they overload-resolve, compare and convert identically. Wanting a genuinely distinct type — a strong typedef — requires an actual class, which is a different tool for a different job.

mcq.prompt: Which use site does *not* require the template argument to be written out?
choices: `Buffer<double> prices{64};` for `template<class T> class Buffer`
`double origin = zero<double>;` for `template<class T> constexpr T zero = T{};`
`int squared = square(7);` for `template<class T> T square(T value)`
`Vec<int> quantities{1, 2, 3};` for `template<class T> using Vec = std::vector<T>`
mcq.explain: A function template can deduce `T` from its arguments, so `square(7)` needs nothing written. A variable template and an alias template have no arguments to deduce from and must be spelled. The class template is the interesting near-miss: CTAD can sometimes deduce class template arguments from *constructor* arguments, but that is a separate C++17 feature rather than the ordinary deduction that makes `square(7)` work.

mcq.section: Deduction: how the compiler picks T
mcq.prompt: For `template<class T> T max(T a, T b);`, why is `max(1, 2.0)` an error?
choices: Because `int` and `double` have different sizes
Because the two arguments propose `int` and `double` for one parameter, and deduction does not convert to reconcile conflicting proposals
Because the return type cannot be deduced from two different parameter types
Because `1` is an lvalue and `2.0` is a prvalue
mcq.explain: Each argument independently proposes a type for `T`, and the proposals must agree exactly before overload resolution continues — deduction finds types, it does not negotiate a compromise. Fixing `T` explicitly with `max<double>(1, 2.0)` changes the situation completely: now both parameters are `double` and ordinary argument conversion turns `1` into `1.0`.

mcq.section: Deduction: how the compiler picks T
mcq.prompt: `auto wrong = max("alpha", "beta");` compiles for `template<class T> T max(T a, T b)`. What does it actually compute?
choices: `max<const char*>`, comparing pointer values rather than characters, with an unspecified result for pointers into unrelated objects
`max<const char[6]>`, comparing arrays element by element
Nothing useful: it is undefined behaviour at run time
The lexicographically greater string, because string literals compare as text
mcq.explain: A string literal used as a by-value argument decays to `const char*`, so `T` is deduced as `const char*` and `<` is the built-in pointer comparison. The relational result for pointers into unrelated objects is unspecified, not undefined — the program is well-formed and simply meaningless. Constructing `std::string` arguments makes lexical comparison the operation actually requested.

mcq.prompt: What is the difference between `std::vector ambiguous{3, 5};` and `std::vector<int> filled(3, 5);`?
choices: `ambiguous` fails to compile because CTAD cannot choose between the constructors
`ambiguous` holds three elements all equal to 5; `filled` holds two elements, 3 and 5
Both hold three elements equal to 5; the first just deduces the element type
`ambiguous` holds two elements, 3 and 5; `filled` holds three elements all equal to 5
mcq.explain: CTAD only supplies the missing template argument — it does not alter constructor overload resolution, including the strong preference braces give to the `std::initializer_list` constructor. So braces mean "these elements" and parentheses reach the count-and-value constructor. This is exactly the case where spelling `int` and choosing the bracket style deliberately makes the intent unmistakable.

mcq.prompt: After `std::vector values{1, 2, 3};`, a later `values.push_back(4.5)` is written. What happens to the deduced type?
choices: The element type becomes a common type of `int` and `double` chosen at the end of the enclosing scope
The vector is re-deduced as `std::vector<double>`
Nothing: deduction belongs to the definition, so `values` remains `std::vector<int>` and 4.5 is converted on insertion
The program is ill-formed, because CTAD forbids later insertions of other types
mcq.explain: CTAD happens once, at the object definition; the type is then fixed and every later operation follows the ordinary `std::vector<int>` interface. The value 4.5 undergoes the usual conversion to `int` on insertion — a narrowing conversion that is easy to miss, which is another reason to spell the element type where a reviewer would otherwise have to reconstruct it.

mcq.prompt: `std::sort(prices.begin(), prices.end())` on a `std::list<int>` produces a wall of diagnostics whose first `error:` points at `__last - __first` inside a library header. How should you triage it?
choices: Start from the last error, since compilers report the root cause last
Read the first `error:`, follow `required from` lines back to the first location in your own source, and ignore library-internal candidates until your call makes sense
Rebuild with the library headers preprocessed so the real error is visible
Assume the standard library is misconfigured, since a correct call cannot fail inside a header
mcq.explain: Later errors are usually consequences of the first, and the useful information is the chain from your call site into the machinery: here `__last - __first` says the iterator type has no subtraction, which is the real diagnosis — `std::sort` needs random access and a list gives bidirectional iterators. The failure is inside a header because that is where the requirement is used, not because anything is misconfigured; concepts turn many such failures into a direct "constraint not satisfied" message.

mcq.prompt: What is a concept, and what does it cost at run time?
choices: A named compile-time predicate on types; nothing at run time
A runtime type check inserted at each constrained call
A base class that constrained types must inherit from
A compile-time predicate that also emits a runtime assertion in debug builds
mcq.explain: A concept is checked entirely by the compiler: it decides whether a template argument is acceptable and improves the diagnostic when it is not, then disappears. The generated code for a constrained template is identical to the unconstrained one. Concepts also require no inheritance relationship — they are structural predicates over expressions, which is what lets them constrain `int` as readily as a user type.

mcq.prompt: In a `requires` expression such as `{ std::hash<T>{}(value) } -> std::convertible_to<std::size_t>;`, what is actually happening?
choices: The expression is evaluated at compile time and must yield a `std::size_t`
The compiler generates a runtime probe that reports failures through an exception
The expression is evaluated once at program start and its result is cached
The compiler checks that the expression is well-formed and that its type satisfies the stated result requirement; the expression is never executed
mcq.explain: Read the body as "for a value of type `T`, these expressions must compile, with these result requirements". Nothing is evaluated — `value` is a parameter of the requires expression that never exists as an object. That is why a `requires` expression can test operations that would be expensive, or that have no meaningful value at all, without any cost.

mcq.section: Function objects and lambda anatomy — the flagship
mcq.prompt: What does a lambda expression create?
choices: A function pointer to a compiler-generated free function
A `std::function` object holding the body
An object of a unique, unnamed compiler-generated class — the closure type — whose `operator()` is the body
An inline block of code with no object identity
mcq.explain: The lambda is a request for a class: captures become data members and the body becomes `operator()`. Because the closure type is unnamed, `auto` is the normal way to hold one. `std::function` can *store* such an object behind a type-erased interface, but that is an extra layer you opt into — a template parameter accepting the concrete closure type needs no wrapper at all.

mcq.section: Function objects and lambda anatomy — the flagship
mcq.prompt: In the hand-written equivalent of `[limit](const Order& o) { return o.price > limit; }`, why is `operator()` marked `const`?
choices: Because the parameter is a `const` reference
Because a lambda's `operator()` is `const` by default, so the closure cannot modify its by-value captures
Because all function objects must have a `const` call operator to be usable by algorithms
Because the capture is by value and by-value captures are stored as `const` members
mcq.explain: A lambda's generated call operator is `const` unless the lambda is declared `mutable`, so the body cannot assign to a by-value capture — the hand-written class must match that to be a faithful model. The members themselves are not `const`; it is the *call operator* that is, which is why `mutable` is enough to lift the restriction.

mcq.section: Function objects and lambda anatomy — the flagship
mcq.prompt: Two lambda expressions with byte-identical source text appear on consecutive lines. What is true of their types?
choices: They have distinct closure types; every lambda expression generates its own
They have the same type only if neither captures anything
Their types are the same after conversion to a function pointer, and different otherwise
They have the same closure type, since the source is identical
mcq.explain: Each lambda *expression* produces its own unique unnamed class, so `std::same_as<decltype(first), decltype(second)>` is false even for identical text. Captureless lambdas do additionally convert to a plain function pointer, and two such pointers can compare equal — but that is a conversion to a shared type, not evidence that the closure types matched.

mcq.prompt: A local `int level = 1;` is captured as `[level]`. The code then sets `level = 2` and calls the closure. What does the closure see?
choices: 2, because captures are read when the closure is called
1 on the first call and 2 on later calls
It is unspecified which value the closure observes
1, because a by-value capture takes its value when the closure is created
mcq.explain: A by-value capture copies into a data member at closure construction; that member is then independent of the original variable. `[&level]` is the form that reads the current outer value on each call — and it is also the form that requires the outer object to still be alive when that call happens.

mcq.prompt: A function has fifteen locals and a global counter. Its lambda writes `[=]` and its body uses two of the locals and the global. What ends up in the closure?
choices: All fifteen locals plus the global
All fifteen locals; globals are never captured
Copies of the two odr-used locals only; the global is accessed directly and not captured
Nothing: `[=]` defers all reads to call time
mcq.explain: A default capture includes only the entities the body actually odr-uses, not every name in scope, and globals and static locals are reached directly so they are never captured at all. The reason to prefer explicit captures anyway is documentation: for a stored, returned, or queued lambda the capture list is where a reader learns what state the object holds and what lifetimes it depends on.

mcq.prompt: `auto make_bad_adder(int n) { return [&n](int x) { return x + n; }; }` — what is the defect?
choices: It fails to compile, because a parameter cannot be captured by reference
The reference capture does not extend `n`'s lifetime, so invoking the returned closure reads a destroyed object: undefined behaviour
It returns a copy of `n` and so is merely wasteful
The closure is fine until it is copied, at which point the reference is rebound
mcq.explain: A reference capture stores a reference, and a reference never keeps its referent alive; `n` dies with the invocation of `make_bad_adder`, leaving the surviving closure pointing into a dead frame. Capturing `[n]` by value fixes it outright. Compiler warnings and AddressSanitizer catch some instances of this, but neither is a lifetime guarantee — the rule is what protects you.

mcq.prompt: A member function stores a lambda written `[=]` into a queue that outlives the object. The body reads a data member. What is the hazard?
choices: `[=]` captures `this` as a pointer, not a copy of the object, so the stored closure can outlive the object and dangle
The member is copied but its `const` is dropped, allowing accidental mutation
The closure copies every member individually, making it too large to queue
None: `[=]` copies the enclosing object, so the closure is self-contained
mcq.explain: Using a member inside a lambda means using `this->member`, and what `[=]` captures is the `this` pointer — one word, by value, pointing at an object with no lifetime commitment to the closure. Queue that closure past the object's death and every member access dangles. The by-value capture being safe is the intuition that makes this bug so easy to write: the capture *is* by value; the pointer it copies is the problem.

mcq.section: Generic lambdas and passing lambdas to algorithms
mcq.prompt: What does declaring a lambda parameter as `auto` do?
choices: It creates a separate closure type for each argument type used
It type-erases the parameter, boxing the argument at each call
It defers the parameter type until link time
It makes the closure's `operator()` a function template, so one closure type can be called with many argument types
mcq.explain: A generic lambda has one closure type whose call operator is a template; each distinct call instantiates a suitable `operator()`. Nothing is boxed or erased — the body is still only valid for types that support the operations it uses, so calling `[](const auto& l, const auto& r){ return l.price < r.price; }` with two `int`s fails exactly as an ordinary template would.

mcq.section: Generic lambdas and passing lambdas to algorithms
mcq.prompt: Why can `std::sort(orders.begin(), orders.end(), less_price)` inline the comparator when passing the same logic through a function pointer often cannot?
choices: Because `std::sort` special-cases closure types in the standard library
Because lambdas are always marked `inline` by the compiler
Because `std::sort` is instantiated with the closure's exact concrete type, so the comparator body is visible inside that instantiation
Because function pointers force an allocation for each call
mcq.explain: The comparator's type is a template parameter, so the instantiation of `std::sort` sees the specific closure type and its body — an ordinary inlining opportunity. A function pointer is a runtime value: unless the optimiser can prove which function it holds, the call site must issue an indirect call it cannot inline through. No allocation is involved either way; that cost belongs to `std::function`.

reading.explain: `[=]` copies only the locals the body odr-uses, and it takes that copy when the closure is created: `budget` is frozen at 2, so the later `budget = 10` is invisible. `calls_made` and `counter` are not locals at all — a global and a static local are reached directly and are never captured — so the closure sees each of them live. `next_id()` therefore yields 101 then 102, giving 202 and 204, and `calls_made` ends at 5 + 2 = 7. The tempting wrong reading is that `[=]` snapshots everything the body touches, which would predict `212 224 5`; the snapshot applies to captures only, and globals and statics are not captures.

reading.section: Deduction: how the compiler picks T
reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: The first argument proposes `T = std::string` (from `std::vector<std::string>`) and the second proposes `T = const char*`, because a string literal used as a by-value argument decays to a pointer. Deduction requires the proposals to agree and will not insert the `const char*`-to-`std::string` conversion to reconcile them, so no candidate survives. The tempting wrong reading is that the literal simply converts, as it would for a non-template parameter declared `std::string` — but conversions apply only after `T` is fixed. Either write `count_matching<std::string>(words, "the")` or give the target its own type parameter.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: `labels` is destroyed when `make_formatter` returns, freeing the heap array that holds the three `std::string` objects. `chosen` was a reference into that array and the closure captured that reference, which never extends a lifetime, so calling `format` reads freed memory: AddressSanitizer reports a heap-use-after-free. The tempting wrong reading is that `chosen` is const and so must be safe, or that the short literal "beta" lives in read-only storage — the small-string buffer lives inside the string object, which lived inside the freed vector. Capturing `[chosen]` by value copies the characters into the closure and removes the dependency.

The generic lambda deduces `key` by value, so the first call decays the literal to `const char*` and `std::pair{key, hits}` is then deduced as `std::pair<const char*, int>` — `a.first` is a pointer, not a string. The second call passes a `std::string`, so `b.first` really is one. Both `emplace_back` calls still build `std::pair<std::string, int>` because the vector's element type is spelled out and fixed, which is why `table.size()` is 2 with two usable entries. The tempting wrong reading is that CTAD looks at what the value is going to be used as; it looks only at the constructor arguments' own types, and an array argument passed by value has already decayed.

The compiler deduces `T` first and checks the constraint afterwards. `route(3)` deduces `T = int`, satisfies `std::integral`, and wins as an exact match over the conversion the `double` overload would need. `route(3.5)` deduces `T = double`, fails the constraint, and the template is removed from the candidate set, leaving the `double` overload. `route(Ticks{7})` deduces `T = Ticks`, which is not integral no matter that `Ticks` converts to `int`; the template drops out and `Ticks` reaches `route(double)` through its user-defined conversion followed by `int`-to-`double`. `route('a')` picks the template, since `std::integral` accepts character types. The tempting wrong reading is that `Ticks` is "an integral type in disguise" — a constraint tests the deduced type itself, never a type it could convert to.

reading.section: Generic lambdas and passing lambdas to algorithms
reading.explain: The comparator captures `words` by reference, so `order` is genuinely sorted by word length: sizes 4, 3, 6, 5 give `order == {1, 0, 3, 2}`. The second `std::sort` then rearranges `words` into `banana fig kiwis pear`, and the saved indices now name entirely different words, so the loop prints `words[1] words[0] words[3] words[2]` — `fig banana pear kiwis`. The tempting wrong reading is `fig pear kiwis banana`, the length order that was true only until `words` moved. A by-reference capture is not the bug here; the bug is that an index is a reference to a position, and the second sort silently changed what each position means.

writing.section: Deduction: how the compiler picks T
writing.prompt: A word-frequency tool needs to count how many entries of a range equal a given value. Write two function templates: `count_exact`, which takes a `std::vector<T>` and a `const T&` so that both arguments must agree on one type, and `count_equal`, which gives the sought value its own independent type parameter. Then write a `demo()` that shows, in comments, which call of `count_exact` fails deduction against a `std::vector<std::string>` searched with a string literal, and gives two different fixes — one that converts the argument and one that fixes the template argument — plus the `count_equal` call that needs no fix at all.
checklist: `count_exact` uses a single type parameter for the element type and the sought value
`count_equal` has two independent type parameters and is callable with a string literal directly
A comment names the failing call and states that deduction will not convert to reconcile `std::string` and `const char*`
One fix converts the argument; a second fix supplies the template argument explicitly
The file compiles as written
writing.notes: The two designs are different interfaces, not two spellings of one. `count_exact` is the stricter contract: it guarantees that the needle has the element type, which matters when `operator==` is heterogeneous or expensive. `count_equal` pushes the comparison onto whatever `value == needle` means, which is what makes the literal work — `std::string` has an `operator==` taking `const char*`. Neither is a workaround for the other.

writing.prompt: Build a small word-frequency facility that uses all four template kinds exactly once. Requirements: an alias template `Counts<Key>` naming the underlying associative container; a variable template giving the zero count for any type; a class template `Histogram<Key>` with `add`, `count` (returning the zero value for an absent key) and read access to its buckets; and a function template `total` that deduces `Key` from its argument. Add a `static_assert` proving the alias names an existing type rather than creating a new one, and a comment marking which use sites deduce their argument and which must spell it.
checklist: All four kinds appear: alias template, variable template, class template, function template
A `static_assert` shows `Counts<Key>` is the same type as the container it aliases
`count` returns the variable template's value for a key that is absent
`total` deduces `Key` from its argument while the `Histogram` object spells it
The file compiles as written
writing.notes: Only the function template deduces here. `Histogram<std::string>` spells its argument because ordinary deduction does not apply to class templates — CTAD could deduce it from constructor arguments, but this class has no constructor that mentions `Key`. The alias and the variable template have no arguments to deduce from at all. The `static_assert` is the point of the alias: `Counts<std::string>` and the map type are one type, so they overload-resolve and convert identically.

writing.prompt: Define a concept `Sized` that a type satisfies when a `const` value of it supports `.size()` convertible to `std::size_t` and `.empty()` convertible to `bool`. Prove with `static_assert`s that it holds for `std::string` and `std::vector<int>` and fails for `int`. Then constrain three functions with it, using a different one of the chapter's three syntaxes each time: `same_length(a, b)`, `widest(items)` over a vector of sized things, and `blank(value)`. Add a comment stating what the constraint costs at run time.
checklist: `Sized` is written as a `requires` expression with two result requirements
Three `static_assert`s cover `std::string`, `std::vector<int>` and the negative case for `int`
The three functions use a constrained template parameter, a `requires` clause, and the abbreviated `auto` form — one each
A comment states that a concept is checked by the compiler and adds no runtime work
The file compiles as written
writing.notes: A `requires` expression is never executed: `value` is a parameter of the expression that never becomes an object, which is what lets a concept probe operations that would be expensive or meaningless to run. Note also the order of events at a call: the compiler deduces a candidate `T` first and only then asks whether `T` satisfies the constraint. That is why `same_length(1, 2)` reports "int does not satisfy Sized" at the call site rather than failing on `1.size()` somewhere inside the body.

writing.section: Function objects and lambda anatomy — the flagship
writing.prompt: A spell-checker filters out words shorter than a configurable minimum. Write `count_if_manual(range, pred)` so that the predicate's concrete type reaches the loop body — it must be a template parameter, not a `std::function`. Then supply the same predicate twice: once as a lambda capturing the minimum by value, and once as a hand-written function-object class that models what the compiler generates for that lambda. Assert with `static_assert` that the closure is the size of its single capture, and have `demo()` return whether the two callables agree.
checklist: The predicate is a template parameter of `count_if_manual`, and `std::function` appears nowhere
The lambda captures the minimum explicitly by value, not through `[=]`
The hand-written class has one data member per capture and a `const` call operator
A `static_assert` compares `sizeof` the closure against `sizeof` its single captured member
Both callables are run over the same range and their results compared
writing.notes: The `const` on the hand-written `operator()` is not decoration: a lambda's call operator is `const` unless the lambda is declared `mutable`, so a faithful model must match it. The `sizeof` assertion holds on ordinary implementations because each by-value capture becomes one unnamed data member, but layout is implementation-defined — an empty closure still has nonzero size, since every complete object needs an addressable identity.

writing.prompt: A log tool needs two callables with opposite lifetime contracts. `make_matcher(pattern)` returns a predicate that must stay valid after the factory returns and after the caller's original pattern is gone. `count_matches(lines, pattern)` creates a callable, consumes it inside the same call, and returns a count. Write both, choosing the capture mode each contract demands, and include as a comment the reference-capturing version of the factory together with a one-line diagnosis of why it is undefined behaviour rather than merely wasteful.
checklist: The returned closure owns its pattern by value
The locally consumed closure captures by reference and a comment justifies why that is safe here
The broken factory appears as a comment naming the destroyed referent
A comment states that a reference capture does not extend the referent's lifetime
The file compiles as written
writing.notes: The rule that decides both cases is where the closure goes, not how big the captured object is. Returned, stored, or queued closures capture by value; a closure consumed inside the call that created it may capture by reference. The failure mode worth remembering is the edit that moves an existing lambda from the second category to the first without anyone revisiting its capture list. Note also that copying a pointer or a view by value copies a lifetime dependency, so a by-value capture is not automatically self-contained.

writing.section: Generic lambdas and passing lambdas to algorithms
writing.prompt: Write `sort_by(range, project)`, which sorts a range in place by a caller-supplied projection. Contract: it must work for any range whose projected keys are ordered by `<`; the projection's type must be a template parameter so its body stays visible to the optimiser; and the comparator handed to `std::sort` must not copy the projection on every comparison. Then demonstrate it with a single generic lambda used on two different element types, plus one type-specific projection, and note in a comment which call the generic lambda would reject.
checklist: `sort_by` takes the projection as a template parameter and passes a comparator to `std::sort`
The comparator captures the projection by reference rather than copying it per comparison
One generic lambda with `const auto&` parameters is used on two different element types
A second, type-specific projection is used on a third range
A comment names a call the generic lambda would reject and why
writing.notes: Two mechanisms combine here. The projection is a template parameter, so `sort_by` and the `std::sort` instantiation it drives both see the concrete closure type and can inline the body — a `std::function` or a function pointer would leave an indirect call the optimiser usually cannot see through. And the generic lambda has one closure type whose `operator()` is a template, so the same object serves `std::string` and `std::vector<int>` without any erasure. Iterator and comparator requirements are formalised in Chapter 13.
